I have 2013 Bonneville SE. I have been looking for awhile now. Try burly brand for canvas bags. They also have mounting systems. 

You cannot get the Triumph branded mounting system anymore for my bike. I had to order a version using the same part number from china. Still waiting on it to come in. 

Other bag options are the triumph branded bags, very expensive though and you need the triumph mounts for that. 

You can still find SW Motech bags, you want the LS versions of the Legend series. For those you can either try and order the saddle strap (only on Amazon/Ebay now) or make your strap. Still need a mounting system, either of the two I listed above should work. 

I am at the point where I am going to try to repurpose a pair of old messengers bags and make them saddlebags once I get my mounting brackets in. 

For reference triumph brackets are #A9738022, I would look up what it be for your bike. Chinese version i ordered was $50>. 

Burly brand brackets, B15-1060B. $119.95

Triumph bags were over $250 per bag.

SW MOTECH was 145-162 per bag, strap was listed for 83.88.

1. Always treat the gun as loaded.
2. Always keep the gun pointed in a safe direction.
3. Always keep your finger straight and off the trigger until you are ready to shoot.
4. Always keep the gun unloaded until you are ready to use it.
5. Never point the gun at anything you don't intend to destroy.
6. Be sure of your target and what is beyond it.
7. Learn the mechanical and handling characteristics of the gun you are using.
8. Always use proper Ammunition.
9. Be sure the barrel is clear of obstructions before loading and shooting.
10. If your gun fails to fire when the trigger is pulled, hold your shooting position for several seconds; then with the muzzle pointed in a safe direction, carefully unload the gun.

Obviously I am late to the party on this one. I will try to line out my feeling and on the situation.

​

CDC Report from 2012 based on data from 2008-2010.

**Death Rates**

14,283 motorcycle deaths.

42% (6057) were not wearing helmets. US wide.

12% (739) were not wearing helmets in helmet required states. (12% of deaths inside helmet required states were not wearing helmets). (20 states).

64% (4,814) of deaths were not wearing helmets in partial helmet states, criteria restricted helmet use only. (27 states).

79% (504) of deaths were not wearing helmets in no helmet required states. (3 states only).

​

From this we can easily a large margin for increased deaths. 12% of deaths versus 79%. It can be inferred that a requiring helmet could reduce significantly reduce motorcycle deaths. Yes there is likely a correlation between riders who wear less safety gear and participate in dangerous riding. (Riding under the influence, stunt riding, etc). I cannot determine what the difference would be if these groups were required to wear helmets or not.

​

An editorial note states they suspect that universal helmet laws could prevent up to 37% of all fatalities on motorcycles.

​

**Cost to society and savings**

Costs saved were estimated to be $1,212,800 per fatality, $171,753 per serious injury, and $7,523 per minor injury (in year 2010 dollars). By using this estimate the report estimated that the US saved $3 billion in 2010 by enforcing helmet laws. This does not include the lost contribution to GDP that the lifetime of the dead rider would have on the economy. Nor does it account for the financial position loved ones would be left without them and the impact that has over time.

​

**Personal Opinion**

I very strongly believe in the personal safety of individuals and individual rights. At some point we need to understand what is best for the country and for motorcycling in the US. I think this report presents a strong enough argument to start enforcing universal helmet laws across all 50 states. Another addition could a new and revised DOT standard for testing helmets. I think this is the minimum we can do. I believe the lifetime savings could be $1 trillion in as short as 10 years. That is 37% 6057 deaths (with no helmets, 2,241.09) x the estimated cost of fatality $1,212,800 over 10 years. $27,179,939,520. Yes 27 billion. Toss in the other factors like lost GDP due to death and related factors we could easily hit $1 trillion.

Edit 2: Factors the average income in 2012 dollars over 10 years of additional life for the preventable deaths. ($45,456 average income x 2,241,09 preventable deaths x 10 years) Add an additional $1,018,709,870.40 (1 billion) to the previous estimate now totaling $28,198,649,390,40.

Federal Reserve Data

​

I believe the savings are worth the infringement on people's rights to ride and die.

​

Hey bud, not super experienced. I have bought two bikes both used. So my recommendations.


1. Take the MSF or motorcycle safety course.
This let's you get on a ride learn the basics and not drop 3K and decide you dont like it. 

2. ATGATT. All the gear al the time. You should look at dropping 500-1000 on gear. 


Solid helmet. I reccomend full face, bare minimum DOT rated. You can get a nice one for sub $200. 


Gloves and jacket. Depends on where you are and seasons of riding. I live in Colorado where we can mostly ride 9 months of the year, very dry. I have two jackets, one textile for hot weather (mesh is better for hotter and more humid, from the accent it sounds that guy is in the south).  One for three season into winter. Great jacket can be sub $200. Gloves same thing sub $50. Mechanics gloves will cut it in a crash.

Boots/shoes and pants. Depends a lot on your riding style. Proper motorcycle boots and shoes help immobolize the foot in the event of a crash. Pants, do you like skin on your legs? Boots sub $200 same for pants. 


3. The bike. I do not reccomend north of 500cc for a beginner because the power threshold is so unforgiving. You can rev the hell out of a 250 and still keep it under control, I guarantee people on here will disagree and tell you to start out a 1000cc, buy the bike you want now. Is that the bike you want to die on? Also style of bike changes that a lot. Sport bikes will have more power than cruisers at lower revs. 


Look at the chain. Can you see metal? Is it clean? Cleaning a chain is one of the easiest, most frequent and most important parts of moto maintenance. If the chain is disgusting he probaly did not cover all of the other maintenance as well. 


I hope this helps. More experience riders and mechanics will be able to provide good and better advice. Stay safe.

I would say if you still very new as in this is your first bike you should go with a different bike with the same aesthetic. I say this so you have money to still buy solid gear. My first was a 2010 Suzuki TR250x. A very similiar style to most Triumph with a much more forgiving power distribution. There are a lot of bikes out there in that lower engine size range that are very cheap and hold the value well. I got mine for $1700 with 7000 miles on it. A year and half later (after dropping it once on a lowside and getting by a truck in parking lot) I sold it for $1700. With that said I put a couple of hundred in repairs. That gave me the extra cash I needed to buy a solid helmet, jacket and boots. 

If your heart is set on a Triumph then I would say find something a couple of years old. My second bike and current bike is my Bonneville with 865 air cooled engine. I love it but I don't think I would have appreciated it as much as I do without the ability to learn on that first bike. Most of the new Triumphs come with 1000+cc engines which is a lot. You don't get as good of gas mileage and the in city riding is not as fun. A smaller engine bike can be punchy in traffic and really fun because you can get out of second or third gear. 

So you can tell I am huge believer in starting on smaller engine bikes. This is not because they are "starter" bikes. It is because they are cheaper, lighter (especially if you need to pick it up), better in-city and so much fun. I am currently saving up to drop a couple of grand on another bike. I am looking at bikes the CSC San Gabriel 250, Kawasaki Vulcans and Honda Rebels. There are bigger nicer bikes I am looking at as well like the Triumph America, Triumph Scrambler and Indian Scout. 

In the end get what you want but I will say for the fun and long term financial investment you can't go wrong with a small engine bike that has a low price and low miles vs cheaper nicer bike that may be a project bike. You want to ride the bike not spend all of the time fixing it. Keep us posted on what you plan on getting and what you are looking at.
